title: Manifolds and bundles
one_line_summary: A from-scratch tour of the topology and differential structure underneath the whole book: sets and open sets, maps and their classification, homeomorphisms, charts and atlases, smooth transition maps and diffeomorphisms (with a proof that diffeomorphism invariance forces the divergence of T to vanish), compactness, curves, tangent vectors as derivations, and a picture-driven introduction to fibre bundles, sections, and the cylinder versus Moebius contrast.
role_in_book: An optional appendix that supplies the foundations the main text deliberately kept in the background. Chapter 31 reintroduced geometry with a light-touch manifold definition and Chapter 33 introduced the Lie derivative (and diffeomorphisms in a margin note), both pointing here for rigour; a Chapter 12 margin note promises that nabla . T = 0 can be justified from diffeomorphism invariance, delivered in Example C.10 using the action machinery of Chapter 40. Chapters 15, 19, 44 and 50 also send readers here for the technical meaning of bundles, topology and compactness. It replaces the embedded pictures used earlier (a sphere sitting in R^3 in Chapter 7, the tangent plane to a surface in Chapter 30) with intrinsic constructions, and prepares readers for modern texts, singularity theory (Chapters 26 and 50) and the bundle language behind gauge fields (Chapter 44). It sits between the conventions appendix (B) and the embedding appendix (D).

assumed_background.topic: Functions of several variables, partial derivatives and the chain rule
Jacobian matrix and determinant of a change of variables
Vector spaces, basis expansion v = v^mu e_mu
Informal manifold picture: locally flat spaces, S^1, S^2, torus, and non-manifold examples
Coordinate transformations and tangent vectors as directional derivatives in coordinates
Lie derivative along a vector field and the formula for L_u g
Action principle, functional derivative with respect to g_{mu nu}, energy-momentum tensor from the matter Lagrangian
Meaning of nabla . T = 0 as local energy-momentum conservation
Integration by parts in curved space (covariant divergence with sqrt(-g))

learning_objectives: Reader can explain why general relativity needs an intrinsic manifold description rather than a surface embedded in a bigger Euclidean space.
Reader can order the layers set, topological space, manifold, and manifold-with-metric, and say what extra structure each layer adds.
Reader can define open ball, open set, open cover and the Hausdorff property in R^n and sketch a non-Hausdorff branching space.
Reader can classify a given real function as many-to-one, one-to-one, onto, or bijective by inspecting its graph, and state when an inverse map exists.
Reader can state the topological definition of continuity and of a homeomorphism, and decide whether pairs such as mug/doughnut, line/circle, disc/square are homeomorphic.
Reader can define a chart, coordinate neighbourhood and atlas, and show why the circle needs at least two charts while R^m needs one.
Reader can write a coordinate transformation as the transition map psi o phi^{-1} and the coordinate representation of a function (f o phi^{-1}) or of a map between manifolds (psi o f o phi^{-1}).

Reader can explain, via f o psi^{-1} = (f o phi^{-1}) o (phi o psi^{-1}), why differentiability on a manifold requires C^infinity-compatible charts, and define a differentiable manifold and maximal atlas.
Reader can decide whether maps like x, x^2, x^3 and a linear map on R^2 are diffeomorphisms, using injectivity, smoothness of the inverse and the Jacobian.
Reader can reproduce the argument that invariance of the matter action under diffeomorphisms generated by an arbitrary vector field implies nabla_mu T^{mu nu} = 0.
Reader can give a working definition of compactness, test it with the sequence 1/n on [0,1] versus (0,1], and list compact and non-compact examples.

Reader can define a tangent vector as the derivative of f o c along a curve, derive its coordinate form with the chain rule, recover components by acting on coordinate functions, and state the linearity and Leibniz properties.
Reader can describe the tangent space at a point as the vector space of equivalence classes of curves sharing a tangent, independent of any embedding.

Reader can describe a fibre bundle by base, fibre, total space and projection, give TS^1 = S^1 x R as a trivial bundle, contrast it with the Moebius bundle, and use sections (pi o s = identity) and the zero section to tell them apart.

teaching_approach.summary: A deliberately 'forget everything and rebuild' appendix. The authors strip away the metric and embedding, then climb a pyramid of structure (set, topology, manifold, metric) one rung at a time. Each abstract definition is paired with a small sketch of blobs and arrows and followed immediately by a numbered example drawn from the line, the circle, the plane or familiar objects (mug, doughnut, globe). The central device is the composition of maps: every coordinate-level object (coordinates, transformations, function values, curves, tangent vectors) is expressed as a composite with the chart map and read aloud in words ('input ... output ...'). Rigour is only partial: formal alternatives are pushed into margin notes, and physics payoffs (gauge symmetry, conservation of T, gauges and bundles) are signposted rather than developed, apart from one worked field-theory example.
narrative_arc: Motivation: spacetime need not sit inside a higher-dimensional Euclidean space, so an intrinsic, smooth description is required; singularities become places where that description fails.

Big picture: split geometry into two ingredients, the smooth manifold and the metric laid on it; flat space, Minkowski spacetime and GR spacetime as manifold plus metric; pyramid figure of layered structure.
Primitive vocabulary: intervals, set operations, R^n with Euclidean distance, open balls, open sets, open covers, Hausdorff property.
Maps as the basic tool: notation, composition, images and inverse images, many-to-one / one-to-one / into / onto / bijection, checked on four graphs.
Structure-preserving maps: topological continuity, homeomorphism, clay-deformation intuition, list of homeomorphic and non-homeomorphic pairs.
Manifold defined as locally homeomorphic to R^n; examples and non-examples.
Coordinates as a homeomorphism from a patch to R^m; the circle forces two patches; charts, atlases and transition maps psi o phi^{-1}; formal manifold definition collected.
Functions and maps on manifolds made concrete through coordinate representations.

Problem: chart-level differentiability is chart dependent; fix by requiring C^infinity transition maps; differentiable manifold, maximal atlas, differentiable maps, diffeomorphisms; tests on simple maps.
Physics payoff: diffeomorphisms as active transformations and gauge symmetries of GR; Lie derivative generated by a flow; Example C.10 derives nabla . T = 0 from diffeomorphism invariance.
Compactness as the generalization of a closed bounded interval, via sequences; examples.

Curves as maps from an interval; tangent vectors as derivatives of f along curves; chain rule gives components and coordinate basis; derivation axioms; equivalence classes of curves; tangent space at each point.

Fibre bundles by picture: rotate tangent lines vertical and lift them off the curve; base, fibre, projection, product bundle, TS^1 as cylinder, Moebius twist, local vs global triviality, sections and the zero section.
Summary bullets re-state manifold, diffeomorphism, compactness, tangent vector and bundle in one line each.
signature_moves: Every composite map is translated into a plain-language input/output sentence immediately after the formula (e.g. put in a coordinate, get a point, get a new coordinate).
Blob-and-arrow diagrams with a boxed R^m panel: the manifold drawn as an irregular region, the chart image drawn as a gridded patch, maps drawn as curved arrows labelled by their composite.

Motivate a structural requirement by exhibiting a failure: the circle's angle coordinate double-counts one point, forcing a second chart; chart-dependent differentiability forces smooth transition maps.
Use a small ladder of test maps (x, x^2, x^3, a shear-like linear map) to separate bijectivity, smoothness and smooth invertibility.
Magnifying-glass pictures to convey 'locally looks like R^n' for circle, sphere and torus.

Build the bundle concept by redrawing a familiar picture (tangent lines on a curve) step by step until it becomes fibres standing above a base, and then use physical rod-and-ring photographs for trivial and twisted bundles.
Push formal alternatives (open-cover compactness, C^k classes, Jacobian computation) into margin notes so the main line stays informal.
Close the loop to physics inside a mathematics appendix: diffeomorphism invariance of the action delivers nabla . T = 0.

sections.title: Opening: why an intrinsic, smooth description
sections.summary: Argues that embedding a curved space in higher-dimensional flat space is a crutch GR cannot rely on, so spacetime must be described intrinsically as a smooth manifold carrying a separately specified metric. Space, Minkowski spacetime and curved spacetime are recast as manifolds with flat or Lorentzian metrics, singularities are characterized as breakdowns of manifold smoothness, and a pyramid (set, topological space, manifold, manifold with metric) frames the appendix. Margin notes add an executive summary.
concepts: singularity as breakdown of the manifold structure
key_moves: Separate geometry into two independent ingredients: the manifold (smoothness) and the metric (lengths and angles).
Identify R^3 with flat d(,), R^4 with eta(,), and a general M with Lorentz g(,) as three instances of manifold-plus-metric.
Announce a from-scratch rebuild in which metric notions are temporarily forgotten.

sections.title: Preliminaries
sections.summary: Distinguishes metric spaces (distances available) from topological spaces (only neighbourhood structure through open subsets). Lists basic notation: open and closed intervals, membership, union, intersection, subset, empty set, R and R^n with Euclidean distance. Defines open balls, open sets as unions of balls, open covers, and the Hausdorff separation property, illustrated by a panel of small sketches including a branching non-Hausdorff space.
key_moves: Euclidean distance (C.1) makes R^n a metric space, which supplies open balls.
Open sets defined by the every-point-has-a-ball criterion, then used as the notion of 'nearby' once the metric is dropped.
Restrict attention to Hausdorff spaces from the outset.

sections.title: Maps and functions
sections.summary: Introduces a map as a rule assigning to each input in one space a unique output in another, with arrow and maps-to notation, real functions of n variables as maps R^n to R, and composition g o f.
key_moves: Notation f: M -> N (C.2) and x |-> f(x) (C.3).
Composition g o f is read as g(f(x)), the operation used throughout the rest of the appendix.

sections.title: One-to-one, into, and onto
sections.summary: Defines image and inverse image and uses them to classify maps as many-to-one, one-to-one, into (defined on the whole domain), onto, and bijective; only bijections have an inverse map. Example C.1 applies the classification to four function graphs.
key_moves: Classify maps by counting inverse images of points.
Tie existence of a genuine inverse map to bijectivity.
Check the classification against graphs: exponential-like, wiggly cubic, flattened cubic, parabola.

sections.title: Continuous maps
sections.summary: Introduces morphisms as structure-preserving maps for comparing spaces and previews the homeomorphism/diffeomorphism pair. Gives the open-set definition of continuity and defines a homeomorphism as a continuous bijection with continuous inverse, pictured as deforming clay without tearing or gluing. Example C.2 lists homeomorphic and non-homeomorphic pairs (disc and square, graph and domain, mug and doughnut; R^m vs R^n, line vs circle).
key_moves: Continuity phrased with open sets only, so it survives without a metric.
Clay-deformation intuition for homeomorphism, flagged as a special case.
Use compactness (defined later) to explain why a line is not homeomorphic to a circle.

sections.title: Manifolds, coordinates, and charts
sections.summary: Defines a manifold as a set whose points each have a neighbourhood homeomorphic to an open subset of R^n, with the circle, sphere and torus as examples and a line through a plane or a double cone as non-examples. Coordinates are a homeomorphism from a patch to R^m; the circle's angle coordinate cannot include the point where 0 and 2 pi coincide, so two patches are needed. Charts, atlases and transition maps are defined and gathered into a formal manifold definition.
key_moves: Points of a manifold exist without coordinates; coordinates are the map x^mu = phi(P) (C.4) with inverse (C.5).
Circle example: excluding one point makes phi_1 one-to-one; a second chart with a different excluded point completes the cover.
A coordinate transformation is the composite psi o phi^{-1} of two chart maps on the overlap (C.6).
Collect the three defining properties: cover, local homeomorphisms, transition maps on overlaps.

sections.title: Functions on the manifold
sections.summary: Explains that the familiar formula y = f(x^1,...,x^m) is really the coordinate representation f o phi^{-1} of a function living on the manifold, and extends this to maps between manifolds, represented by psi o f o phi^{-1} between two coordinate spaces (Example C.7).
key_moves: Pull a function back to coordinate space by composing with the inverse chart (C.7).
Sandwich a manifold-to-manifold map between two charts (C.8).

sections.title: Differentiation on the manifold
sections.summary: Shows that differentiability judged in one chart need not hold in another unless the transition map is differentiable, leading to C^infinity-related charts, the maximal atlas, and the differentiable manifold. Defines differentiable maps and diffeomorphisms, tests x, x^2, x^3 and a linear map on R^2, and contrasts homeomorphism (continuous deformation) with diffeomorphism (smooth deformation). Diffeomorphisms of a manifold to itself are identified with active transformations and gauge symmetries of GR and underlie the Lie derivative; Example C.10 derives nabla . T = 0 from diffeomorphism invariance of the matter action.
concepts: Lie derivative as generator of a diffeomorphism
conservation of energy-momentum from diffeomorphism invariance
key_moves: Decompose f o psi^{-1} = (f o phi^{-1}) o (phi o psi^{-1}) (C.9) to locate where differentiability can fail.
Require phi_i o phi_j^{-1} to be C^infinity on every overlap (C.10).
Diffeomorphism: invertible map whose coordinate representation and its inverse are both C^infinity; forces equal dimensions.
x^3 is a smooth bijection but not a diffeomorphism because its inverse is not smooth at 0.
Set the metric variation equal to the Lie derivative 2 u_(mu;nu), use symmetry, integrate by parts, invoke arbitrariness of u and the action definition of T.

sections.title: Compact regions
sections.summary: Generalizes the closed interval to compactness: a compact region does not run off to infinity and is missing neither interior pieces nor boundary pieces, made precise by requiring sequences to have accumulation points inside. Example C.11 contrasts [0,1] with (0,1] using 1/n; the Heine-Borel theorem and the closed-and-bounded criterion are cited; Example C.12 lists compact (closed disc, sphere, torus) and non-compact (plane, open disc, punctured disc) spaces. Margin notes give the open-cover definition.
key_moves: Three failure modes of compactness (escaping to infinity, holes, missing boundary).
Sequence test with 1/n shows the removed endpoint breaks compactness.
Note that boundedness needs a metric, so the closed-and-bounded criterion is a Euclidean statement.

sections.title: Curves
sections.summary: Defines a curve as a map from a parameter interval into the manifold and its coordinate description as the composite of the curve with a chart (C.16).
key_moves: Curve c: [a,b] -> M; coordinates along it x^mu = phi o c(lambda).

sections.title: Tangent spaces
sections.summary: Rejects arrows as the basic picture of vectors on a manifold and defines a tangent vector at a point as the rate of change of arbitrary functions along a curve. Splitting f o c through the chart and applying the chain rule yields components dx^mu/dlambda and coordinate basis operators partial/partial x^mu (C.20); acting on coordinate functions recovers the components (Example C.13). Tangent vectors are characterized as linear, Leibniz-obeying maps on smooth functions, identified with equivalence classes of curves, and collected into the tangent space at each point.
key_moves: Rate of change of f(c(lambda)) at lambda = 0 (C.17).
Insert the identity phi^{-1} o phi to write f o c = (f o phi^{-1}) o (phi o c) (C.18).
Chain rule separates curve data (components) from function data (partial derivatives) (C.19, C.20).
Two curves through P with equal coordinate velocities define the same vector (C.23, C.24).

sections.title: Fibre bundles
sections.summary: Builds the bundle idea by rotating the tangent lines of a curve to stand vertically and lifting them off, giving a copy of a fibre above every base point. Defines base space, fibre, total space (dimension equal to the sum), canonical projection, and product (trivial) bundles; TS^1 is the cylinder S^1 x R with coordinates (theta, y). The Moebius bundle is locally a product but globally twisted. Cross sections (lifts with pi o s = identity) generalize graphs of functions, and the necessary crossing of the zero section distinguishes the Moebius bundle from the cylinder. A short chapter summary closes the appendix.
key_moves: Picture tangent vectors as beads on vertical fibres above the base.
Projection pi forgets the fibre coordinate.
TS^1 = S^1 x R with v = y partial_theta.
Glue two locally trivial pieces with a flip to get the Moebius strip.
Sections: s followed by pi is the identity; every section of the twisted bundle must hit zero.

concepts.name: embedding versus intrinsic description
concepts.definition: A space can be studied by placing it inside a larger flat space (extrinsic, embedded) or purely through structures defined on the space itself (intrinsic); GR adopts the intrinsic view because there is no evidence spacetime sits inside a higher-dimensional Euclidean space.
concepts.how_introduced: Opening paragraph: a sphere is usually pictured inside 3D space, but spacetime cannot be assumed to have such a host; the tangent-plane picture of earlier chapters is contrasted with the intrinsic tangent space in Fig. C.15.
concepts.notes: Appendix D takes up embeddings explicitly.

concepts.name: manifold
concepts.definition: A set in which every point has an open neighbourhood that is homeomorphic to an open subset of R^n; equivalently a space covered by charts whose images are open sets of R^n. (Standard definitions also require Hausdorff and second-countable topology.)
concepts.how_introduced: Working definition 'locally flat and Euclidean' in the opening, then a precise local-homeomorphism definition in §C.5 illustrated with magnifying glasses on a circle, sphere and torus, and finally a three-property chart-based definition.
formulas: \forall P\in\mathcal M\ \exists U\ni P \text{ open},\ \phi:U\to\phi(U)\subset\mathbb R^n \text{ homeomorphism}
concepts.notes: The book allows 'for some n', silently permitting different dimensions at different points; it also omits second countability.

concepts.name: pseudo-Riemannian manifold
concepts.definition: A differentiable manifold equipped with a smooth symmetric non-degenerate metric tensor g; in GR the metric has Lorentzian signature and, together with its compatible connection, fixes lengths, angles, causal structure and curvature.
concepts.how_introduced: Placed at the apex of the pyramid of structure (set, topology, manifold, metric) in Fig. C.1; flat space and Minkowski spacetime are presented as special cases.

concepts.name: singularity as breakdown of the manifold structure
concepts.definition: A singularity is characterized as a place where spacetime can no longer be described as a smooth manifold.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned in the opening as a motivation for caring about smoothness; margin note points to black-hole and cosmological singularity studies.

concepts.name: metric space
concepts.definition: A set together with a distance function assigning a non-negative number to each pair of points (symmetric, zero only for equal points, obeying the triangle inequality).
concepts.how_introduced: First line of §C.1, as the richer of two kinds of space; R^n with Euclidean distance is the example.
concepts.notes: The book does not state the metric-space axioms; this is a different use of 'metric' from the metric tensor g.

concepts.name: topological space
concepts.definition: A set together with a collection of subsets declared open (closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections, containing the empty set and the whole space), which encodes nearness without distances.
concepts.how_introduced: Contrasted with a metric space in §C.1: less structure, neighbourhoods described via open subsets; second rung of the pyramid in Fig. C.1.
concepts.notes: The axioms are not given in the book.

concepts.name: open and closed intervals
concepts.definition: (a,b) is the set of reals strictly between a and b; [a,b] also includes the endpoints.
concepts.how_introduced: First bullet of §C.1 with sketches of bracket and parenthesis symbols; later reused as the model for compactness.

concepts.name: Euclidean space R^n
concepts.definition: The set of ordered n-tuples of real numbers with the Euclidean distance; the model space that manifolds resemble locally and in which coordinates live.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in §C.1 with the distance formula, and reintroduced in §C.5 as 'the space where vectors live'.

concepts.name: open ball
concepts.definition: The set of points of R^n lying at distance strictly less than r from a centre y.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined right after the distance formula as the basic example of an open subset, with a dashed circle in a square as picture.

concepts.name: open set
concepts.definition: A subset S of R^n such that each of its points is the centre of some open ball contained in S; equivalently a union of open balls. In a general topological space open sets are the specified collection.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.1 bullet: any region without its boundary is open; open sets are the currency of topology once distances are dropped.

concepts.name: open cover
concepts.definition: A collection of open sets whose union contains a given set A, so that every point of A lies in at least one member.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.1 with a sketch of overlapping dashed discs; reused in a margin note for the open-cover definition of compactness and implicitly by the chart cover of a manifold.
concepts.notes: The book's wording ('every point in A is in the collection O') should be read as 'in some member of O'.

concepts.name: Hausdorff property
concepts.definition: Any two distinct points possess disjoint open neighbourhoods; excludes pathological spaces such as a line that branches or a line with a doubled point.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.1 bullet with a branching picture of a non-Hausdorff space; the authors restrict to Hausdorff spaces thereafter.
concepts.notes: The parenthetical gloss about infinite subdivision of a line is not an accurate characterization; the separation statement is the definition.

concepts.name: map
concepts.definition: A rule f: M -> N assigning to each element of the domain M exactly one element of N.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.2 as the fundamental tool for relating spaces, with a two-blob arrow picture; margin note says map and function are used interchangeably.

concepts.name: composition of maps
concepts.definition: Given f: M -> N and g: N -> L, the composite g o f: M -> L sends x to g(f(x)).
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in §C.2 and then used as the workhorse for coordinates, transformations, function representations, curves and tangent vectors.

concepts.name: image and inverse image
concepts.definition: For a map f and subset S of the domain, f(S) is the set of outputs; the inverse image of T is the set of domain points mapped into T.
concepts.how_introduced: Start of §C.3, used to classify maps.

concepts.name: injective map
concepts.definition: A map in which distinct inputs always give distinct outputs, so every image point has a single inverse-image point.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.3 classification with arrow pictures; margin note gives the synonym and etymology.

concepts.name: surjective map
concepts.definition: A map whose image is the whole target space, so every target point has at least one inverse image.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.3 bullet with French 'sur' etymology in a margin note; contrasted with the book's 'into', which only requires the map to be defined on all of M.
concepts.notes: Some texts use 'into' to mean injective; GA uses it to mean defined on the whole domain.

concepts.name: bijection
concepts.definition: A map that is both one-to-one and onto; exactly these maps have an inverse map, which is itself bijective.
concepts.how_introduced: End of §C.3, then Example C.1 tests four graphs.

concepts.name: morphism
concepts.definition: A map between two mathematical structures that respects the structure in question, used to decide when spaces are 'the same' for some purpose.
concepts.how_introduced: Opening of §C.4 as the general idea behind homeomorphism (topology) and diffeomorphism (smoothness).

concepts.name: continuous map (topological definition)
concepts.definition: phi: M -> N is continuous at x if for every open set V containing phi(x) there is an open set U containing x with phi(U) inside V; continuous means continuous at every point.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated in §C.4 using only open sets so it does not need distances.
concepts.notes: Reduces to the epsilon-delta definition in R^n.

concepts.name: homeomorphism
concepts.definition: A bijection between spaces that is continuous with a continuous inverse; homeomorphic spaces share all topological properties.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.4 with the modelling-clay picture (no tearing, punching holes, gluing or healing), Fig. C.6 mug-to-doughnut, and Example C.2 list of yes/no cases; used next to define manifolds and coordinates.
concepts.notes: A margin note stresses that continuous deformation is only one instance; homeomorphisms can act between non-manifolds.

concepts.name: coordinate function
concepts.definition: A homeomorphism phi from an open patch U of an m-dimensional manifold onto an open subset of R^m; its m component functions x^mu(P) are the coordinates of P.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.5: points of the manifold exist independently of labels; to name them with numbers we map a patch into R^m (Fig. C.8), with the warning that x denotes both the functions and their values.

concepts.name: coordinate neighbourhood
concepts.definition: The open subset U of the manifold on which a given coordinate function is defined and one-to-one.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.5: needed because a single homeomorphism usually cannot cover the whole manifold, as the circle shows.

concepts.name: chart
concepts.definition: A pair (U, phi) of an open set of the manifold and a homeomorphism from U onto an open subset of R^m.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in §C.5 after the circle examples; margin note says physicists call it a coordinate system.

concepts.name: atlas
concepts.definition: A collection of charts whose domains together cover the manifold.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.5 after Examples C.4-C.5: two angle charts with different excluded points cover the circle; Example C.6 contrasts R^m (one chart) with S^1 (at least two).

concepts.name: transition map
concepts.definition: For overlapping charts (U, phi) and (V, psi), the map psi o phi^{-1} from phi(U cap V) to psi(U cap V) that converts one set of coordinates of a point into the other.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.5 via Fig. C.10: go from coordinates back to the point with phi^{-1}, then forward with psi; then built into the formal manifold definition and, in §C.7, required to be smooth.
concepts.notes: The bullet list on p.571 states the direction of phi_i o phi_j^{-1} backwards.

concepts.name: coordinate representation of a function
concepts.definition: A function f: M -> R is handled in practice through f o phi^{-1}, an ordinary real function of the m coordinates on phi(U); similarly a map f: M -> N is represented by psi o f o phi^{-1} between coordinate spaces.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.6: we only have access to coordinates, so we route the input through the inverse chart (Fig. C.11); Example C.7 extends it to manifold-to-manifold maps (Fig. C.12).

concepts.name: C^k and smooth functions
concepts.definition: A function on an open region of R^n is C^k if all partial derivatives of order up to k exist and are continuous; C^infinity (smooth) if this holds for every k.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note in §C.7 with polynomials as smooth and x^{1/3} as a counterexample whose derivative blows up at the origin.

concepts.name: compatible (C^infinity-related) charts
concepts.definition: Two charts are compatible if on their overlap the transition maps in both directions are infinitely differentiable.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.7: a function can look differentiable in one chart and not in another; the decomposition f o psi^{-1} = (f o phi^{-1}) o (phi o psi^{-1}) shows the transition map must be smooth.

concepts.name: maximal atlas
concepts.definition: The atlas containing every chart compatible with a given smooth atlas; fixing it removes spurious distinctions between the same manifold described by different atlases.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.7 immediately after compatibility; Example C.8 uses the maximal atlas containing the identity on R.

concepts.name: differentiable manifold
concepts.definition: A manifold together with a maximal atlas of mutually C^infinity-compatible charts, so that smoothness of functions, curves and maps is chart independent.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.7 as the fix for chart-dependent differentiability; simplest example R with the identity chart (Example C.8).

concepts.name: differentiable map between manifolds
concepts.definition: f: M -> N is differentiable if for all charts (U, phi) of M and (V, psi) of N its representation psi o f o phi^{-1} from R^m to R^n is differentiable.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.7, reusing the sandwich picture of Fig. C.12.

concepts.name: diffeomorphism
concepts.definition: A bijective smooth map between differentiable manifolds whose inverse is also smooth; diffeomorphic manifolds have equal dimension and are regarded as the same smooth manifold.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.7 after differentiable maps, tested on x, x^2, x^3 and a linear map of R^2 (Example C.9), and contrasted with homeomorphism as smooth versus continuous deformation; then related to GR's gauge freedom.

concepts.name: Jacobian determinant
concepts.definition: The determinant of the matrix of partial derivatives of a map's component functions; a non-zero value at a point guarantees local smooth invertibility there (inverse function theorem).
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note in Example C.9 computes 5/4 for phi(x,y) = (x + y/2, y - x/2).
concepts.notes: Non-zero Jacobian everywhere gives only local invertibility; the linear example is globally invertible because it is linear.

concepts.name: active coordinate transformation
concepts.definition: A transformation that moves points of the manifold to other points (as opposed to relabelling the same point); a diffeomorphism from a manifold to itself is its most general smooth form.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.7 discussion of why diffeomorphisms matter for GR, and restated in the chapter summary.

concepts.name: diffeomorphism invariance
concepts.definition: Physical content of GR is unchanged when all fields are pushed along by a diffeomorphism of spacetime to itself; configurations related this way describe the same physics, so diffeomorphisms are the gauge symmetries of the theory.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.7: if moving points with a diffeomorphism leaves the physics unchanged, the moved and unmoved configurations are indistinguishable; used in Example C.10.

concepts.name: Lie derivative as generator of a diffeomorphism
concepts.definition: The one-parameter family of diffeomorphisms obtained by flowing along the integral curves of a vector field u has u as its generator, and the Lie derivative L_u measures the first-order change of a tensor under that flow; for the metric (L_u g)_{mu nu} = 2 u_(mu;nu) with a metric-compatible connection.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.7 remark that the Lie derivative of Chapter 33 is most generally defined via diffeomorphisms, with the metric formula recalled in a margin note for Example C.10.

concepts.name: Killing vector field
concepts.definition: A vector field whose flow is an isometry, so L_u g = 0; each one yields a conserved quantity along geodesics.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note in §C.7: because the Lie derivative is built from diffeomorphisms, so is the notion of Killing vectors.
prerequisites: Lie derivative as generator of a diffeomorphism

concepts.name: conservation of energy-momentum from diffeomorphism invariance
concepts.definition: If the matter action is unchanged when the metric is varied by the Lie derivative along any vector field (and the matter fields obey their equations of motion), then the energy-momentum tensor defined from the action has vanishing covariant divergence.
concepts.how_introduced: Example C.10 in §C.7, fulfilling a promise made in Chapter 12 and using the variational definition of T from Chapter 40.
prerequisites: Lie derivative as generator of a diffeomorphism
concepts.notes: The book does not mention that the matter field equations must hold for the argument to go through.

concepts.name: energy-momentum tensor from the action
concepts.definition: T^{mu nu} equals 2/sqrt(-g) times the functional derivative of sqrt(-g) L_m with respect to g_{mu nu}.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted from Chapter 40 in Example C.10.

concepts.name: compactness
concepts.definition: A region is compact if every sequence in it has an accumulation point lying in the region (for metric spaces equivalent to: every open cover has a finite subcover); in R^n this means closed and bounded.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.8 as the upgrade of a closed interval: no escape to infinity, no missing interior pieces, no missing boundary; tested with 1/n on [0,1] and (0,1]; the open-cover version is in a margin note.
concepts.notes: Used back in Example C.2 to show a line is not homeomorphic to a circle.

concepts.name: Heine-Borel theorem
concepts.definition: A subset of R (or R^n) is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded; in particular closed intervals are compact.
concepts.how_introduced: Cited without proof in §C.8 with a pointer to Spivak.

concepts.name: bounded set
concepts.definition: A set that lies within some finite distance of a point; the notion requires a metric.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note in §C.8 accompanying the closed-and-bounded criterion.

concepts.name: parametrized curve on a manifold
concepts.definition: A map c from an interval of real parameter values into the manifold; its coordinate description is phi o c, giving x^mu(lambda).
concepts.how_introduced: §C.9 with Fig. C.13, as the ingredient needed to define tangent vectors.

concepts.name: tangent vector as directional derivative
concepts.definition: At P = c(0), the tangent vector of curve c acts on any smooth function f by returning d(f o c)/dlambda at lambda = 0; in coordinates it is v = (dx^mu/dlambda) partial/partial x^mu.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.10: arrows are unavailable on a manifold (no origin or straightness), so a vector is defined by what it does to functions; the chain rule through a chart gives the coordinate form (Fig. C.14).

concepts.name: derivation
concepts.definition: A map v from smooth functions to real numbers at a point that is linear and satisfies the product (Leibniz) rule; at each point derivations are in one-to-one correspondence with tangent vectors.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.10 'firming up' the definition after Example C.13.

concepts.name: coordinate basis vectors
concepts.definition: The derivative operators partial/partial x^mu at a point, which form a basis of the tangent space associated with a chart; components are then v^mu = dx^mu/dlambda.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off from the chain-rule expression (C.19)-(C.20), with the order of factors swapped to match v = v^mu e_mu.

concepts.name: equivalence class of curves
concepts.definition: Curves through the same point whose coordinate velocities agree at that point are identified; each tangent vector corresponds to one such class.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.10 via (C.23)-(C.24): many curves share a velocity, so a vector cannot be tied to one particular curve.

concepts.name: tangent space
concepts.definition: The vector space of all tangent vectors at a point P of the manifold, with dimension equal to that of the manifold; there is a separate one at each point.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.10: tangent vectors are said to live not in the manifold but in a space 'floating above' each point (Fig. C.15a), contrasted with the embedded tangent plane of earlier chapters (Fig. C.15b).

concepts.name: fibre bundle
concepts.definition: A manifold B built from a base manifold M and a fibre manifold V, with a continuous projection onto M such that the preimage of each base point is a copy of V and small regions look like products; dim B = dim M + dim V.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.11 by redrawing the tangent lines of a curve as non-intersecting vertical lines and lifting them above the curve (Figs. C.16-C.17); margin note in §C.10 anticipates it.

concepts.name: base space and fibre
concepts.definition: The base space is the manifold M over which a bundle is built; the fibre is the manifold V of which one copy stands above each base point.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.11 following the lifting construction; tangent vectors at a point pictured as beads on its fibre.

concepts.name: canonical projection
concepts.definition: The continuous map pi: B -> M sending every point of a fibre to the base point it lies over, forgetting the fibre coordinate.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.11 as undoing the lifting construction (Figs. C.17-C.18).

concepts.name: tangent bundle
concepts.definition: The bundle whose fibre over each point is the tangent space there; a point of TM is a point of M together with a tangent vector at it, so dim TM = 2 dim M.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.11 as the motivating special case, with TS^1 as the cylinder in Example C.14 and Fig. C.19.

concepts.name: trivial (product) bundle
concepts.definition: A bundle that is globally the Cartesian product M x V, whose points are pairs (a, b) with a in M and b in V.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.11 with a grid-rectangle picture (Fig. C.18); TS^1 = S^1 x R is the cylinder example.

concepts.name: local versus global triviality
concepts.definition: Every bundle looks like a product over small enough regions of the base (local triviality); it is globally trivial only if a single product description works over the whole base. A twisted bundle is locally but not globally a product.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.11 posed as a question after TS^1, answered by the Moebius example: cutting out a base point leaves something deformable to a cylinder, but gluing the two pieces with a flip does not.
concepts.notes: The book's phrase that bundles are locally trivial 'if they are formed from a product space' blurs the definition; local triviality is part of what a bundle is.

concepts.name: Moebius bundle
concepts.definition: The real line bundle over the circle obtained by gluing the ends of a strip with a reversal of the fibre direction; locally a product, globally not diffeomorphic to the cylinder.
concepts.how_introduced: Example C.15 with a photograph of rods on a ring tilting through a half turn (Fig. C.20b).

concepts.name: cross section
concepts.definition: A continuous map s: M -> B choosing one point on each fibre, so that projecting back gives the identity: pi o s = I; for a product bundle it is the graph of a V-valued function on M, and for a tangent bundle it is a vector field.
concepts.how_introduced: §C.11 formal characterization of bundles, pictured as a wavy loop around a cylinder with upward lift arrows from the base (Fig. C.21).
concepts.notes: The book does not say explicitly that sections of the tangent bundle are vector fields; this is the key link to physics.

concepts.name: zero section
concepts.definition: The section of a vector bundle that picks the zero vector in every fibre.
concepts.how_introduced: Example C.16: any section of the Moebius bundle must meet it, while a section of the cylinder can avoid it, which distinguishes the two bundles.

concepts.name: gauge fields as bundle structures
concepts.definition: Gauge theories are naturally formulated with fields as sections of bundles over spacetime and potentials as connections on those bundles.
concepts.how_introduced: Only signposted in the opening paragraph as the reason bundles appear at the end of the appendix.

key_equations.label: (C.1)
key_equations.name: Euclidean distance in R^n
key_equations.meaning: Makes R^n a metric space; used to define open balls and hence open sets.
key_equations.symbols: x, y points of R^n with components x^mu, y^mu

key_equations.name: Open ball
key_equations.meaning: The basic open set; open sets are unions of these.

key_equations.label: (C.2)
key_equations.name: Map notation
key_equations.meaning: f takes elements of M to elements of N.

key_equations.label: (C.3)
key_equations.name: Map on elements
key_equations.meaning: Element-level statement of the same map.

key_equations.name: Composition
key_equations.meaning: Chaining maps, the core operation of the appendix.
key_equations.symbols: f: M -> N, g: N -> L

key_equations.label: (C.4)
key_equations.name: Coordinates of a point
key_equations.meaning: A chart map turns a point of the manifold into an m-tuple of numbers.
key_equations.symbols: phi coordinate function on U, P a point in U

key_equations.label: (C.5)
key_equations.name: Point from coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Because phi is a homeomorphism it can be inverted: coordinates determine a unique point of U.

key_equations.label: (C.6)
key_equations.name: Coordinate transformation as transition map
key_equations.meaning: The coordinates of the same point in a second chart are obtained by going back to the manifold with phi^{-1} and out again with psi.
key_equations.symbols: (U, phi), (V, psi) overlapping charts; x^mu, y^mu the two coordinate labels of P

key_equations.name: Transition maps in the formal definition (corrected direction)
key_equations.meaning: On each overlap the composite of one chart with the inverse of another maps between open subsets of R^m.

key_equations.label: (C.7)
key_equations.name: Coordinate representation of a function
key_equations.meaning: What we usually write as f(x^1,...,x^m) is the manifold function f composed with the inverse chart.
key_equations.symbols: f: M -> R, phi chart on U

key_equations.label: (C.8)
key_equations.name: Coordinate representation of a map between manifolds
key_equations.meaning: A map between manifolds becomes an ordinary tuple-valued function between coordinate spaces once sandwiched between charts.
key_equations.symbols: (U, phi) chart on M, (V, psi) chart on N

key_equations.label: (C.9)
key_equations.name: Chart change for a function
key_equations.meaning: Shows that differentiability of a function in one chart transfers to another chart only if the transition map is differentiable.

key_equations.label: (C.10)
key_equations.name: Smooth compatibility condition
key_equations.meaning: Defines C^infinity-related charts; a maximal atlas of such charts makes the manifold differentiable.

key_equations.name: Differentiable map between manifolds
key_equations.latex: \psi\circ f\circ\phi^{-1}:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n\ \text{differentiable for all charts}
key_equations.meaning: Chart-level criterion for smoothness of maps between manifolds.
key_equations.symbols: m, n dimensions of M and N

key_equations.name: Diffeomorphism condition
key_equations.latex: y=\psi\circ f\circ\phi^{-1}(x)\in C^\infty,\qquad x=\phi\circ f^{-1}\circ\psi^{-1}(y)\in C^\infty
key_equations.meaning: A diffeomorphism is invertible with both the map and its inverse smooth in coordinates; this forces m = n.

key_equations.name: Jacobian of the test map in Example C.9
key_equations.meaning: Non-vanishing Jacobian of a linear map of R^2 shows it is invertible and hence a diffeomorphism.

key_equations.label: (C.11)
key_equations.name: Variation of the matter action with the metric
key_equations.meaning: First-order change of the matter action when the metric components change.
key_equations.symbols: g determinant of the metric, L_m matter Lagrangian density

key_equations.label: (C.12)
key_equations.name: Lie derivative of the metric (margin note, indices corrected)
key_equations.meaning: Change of the metric under the flow generated by u; the first term vanishes for a metric-compatible connection, leaving the symmetrized covariant derivative.
key_equations.symbols: u generating vector field; parentheses denote symmetrization with a 1/2

key_equations.name: Metric variation generated by a diffeomorphism
key_equations.meaning: Infinitesimal diffeomorphisms change the metric by the Lie derivative along their generator.

key_equations.label: (C.13)
key_equations.name: Diffeomorphism invariance condition
key_equations.meaning: Invariance of the action under the metric change; the symmetrization is dropped because the functional derivative is symmetric (factor 2 absorbed into the zero).

key_equations.label: (C.14)
key_equations.name: After integration by parts
key_equations.meaning: Moving the derivative off u (discarding a boundary term) leaves u times a covariant divergence; since u is arbitrary the bracketed divergence must vanish.

key_equations.label: (C.15)
key_equations.name: Energy-momentum tensor from the action
key_equations.meaning: Definition quoted from Chapter 40; identifies the bracket in (C.14) with T/2.

key_equations.name: Conservation law
key_equations.meaning: Result of Example C.10: local energy-momentum conservation follows from diffeomorphism invariance of the matter action.

key_equations.label: (C.16)
key_equations.name: Coordinates along a curve
key_equations.meaning: A curve on the manifold, viewed through a chart, becomes an ordinary parametrized curve in R^m.

key_equations.label: (C.17)
key_equations.name: Rate of change along a curve
key_equations.meaning: The basic ingredient of a tangent vector: how fast a function changes as one moves along the curve through P = c(0).

key_equations.label: (C.18)
key_equations.name: Splitting through the chart
key_equations.meaning: Inserting the identity phi^{-1} o phi separates the function's coordinate representation from the curve's coordinate representation.

key_equations.label: (C.19)
key_equations.name: Chain rule on the manifold
key_equations.meaning: Ordinary multivariable chain rule applied to the two coordinate representations.

key_equations.label: (C.20)
key_equations.name: Tangent vector in coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Defines the tangent vector: components are the coordinate velocities of the curve and basis vectors are partial derivative operators, matching v = v^mu e_mu.

key_equations.label: (C.21)
key_equations.name: Coordinate function along the curve
key_equations.meaning: The nu-th coordinate evaluated along the curve, used as the test function in Example C.13.
key_equations.symbols: phi^nu nu-th component of the chart map

key_equations.label: (C.22)
key_equations.name: Vector acting on a coordinate
key_equations.meaning: Feeding a coordinate function to the vector returns its nu-th component, because partial x^nu/partial x^mu is a Kronecker delta.

key_equations.name: Derivation axioms
key_equations.meaning: Coordinate-free characterization of tangent vectors at a point as linear maps on smooth functions obeying the product rule.
key_equations.symbols: alpha, beta real numbers; f, g in C^infinity(M); functions evaluated at P

key_equations.label: (C.23)
key_equations.name: Curves through the same point
key_equations.meaning: First condition for two curves to define the same tangent vector.

key_equations.label: (C.24)
key_equations.name: Equal coordinate velocities
key_equations.meaning: Second condition; together with (C.23) defines the equivalence class of curves identified with a tangent vector.

key_equations.name: Dimension of a bundle
key_equations.meaning: The total space has the dimensions of base and fibre added.

key_equations.name: Tangent vector on the circle
key_equations.meaning: Coordinates (theta, y) on TS^1: position on the circle and amplitude along the fibre.
key_equations.symbols: theta angle on S^1, y fibre coordinate

key_equations.label: (C.25)
key_equations.name: Section condition
key_equations.meaning: Lifting the base into the bundle and projecting back returns every base point to itself.
key_equations.symbols: s: M -> B section, pi: B -> M projection, I identity on M

key_equations.label: (C.26)
key_equations.name: Summary definition of a tangent vector
key_equations.meaning: Chapter-summary restatement of the derivative-along-a-curve definition.

figures.caption_paraphrase: Appendix badge (no caption).
figures.visual_description: A large bold black capital letter C on a plain light-grey background: the appendix identifier tile from the opening page layout.
figures.what_it_teaches: Nothing conceptual; page decoration.

redesign.idea: None; decorative chapter tile.
redesign.interaction: None.

figures.label: Fig. C.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: The manifold-with-metric sits on top of a stack of increasingly structured mathematical notions.
figures.visual_description: Four stacked rectangles forming a stepped pyramid. From the widest at the bottom upward they read: Set; Topological space; Manifold M; and at the narrow top (M, g).
figures.what_it_teaches: Geometry is layered: each rung adds structure (open sets, local Euclidean charts and smoothness, then a metric) to the one below.

redesign.idea: Clickable structure ladder: each layer expands into what it adds, which questions become answerable (is it connected? can we differentiate? how long is this curve?), and which example objects qualify.
redesign.interaction: Learner clicks a layer or drags a sample object (branching line, double cone, sphere with round metric) up the ladder; the ladder highlights the highest level the object reaches and explains the failing condition.

figures.label: Fig. C.2 (a)-(d)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Open interval, closed interval, union of two sets, and intersection of two sets.
figures.visual_description: Vector line art that the image export dropped (checked on the page render): (a) a horizontal line cut by two outward-facing round parentheses for an open interval; (b) the same line with square brackets for a closed interval; (c) two overlapping ellipses A and B, both hatched to show the union; (d) the same two overlapping ellipses with only their overlap marked, for the intersection.
figures.what_it_teaches: Notation for intervals and basic set operations.

redesign.idea: Venn and interval playground: two draggable shapes with a selector for union, intersection, subset; an interval with toggleable endpoint brackets.
redesign.interaction: Learner toggles open/closed endpoints and drags sets; the shaded region and the symbolic expression update together.

figures.label: Fig. C.2 (e)
figures.caption_paraphrase: A is a subset of B.
figures.visual_description: A small ellipse labelled A drawn completely inside a larger ellipse labelled B, unshaded.
figures.what_it_teaches: Subset notation A inside B.

redesign.idea: Merge into the set-operations playground above.
redesign.interaction: Drag A; indicator shows whether A is still a subset of B.

figures.label: Fig. C.2 (f)
figures.caption_paraphrase: An open ball in the plane.
figures.visual_description: A square frame representing R^2 containing a dashed circle; the dashing signals that the boundary circle is excluded.
figures.what_it_teaches: Open balls exclude their boundary; dashed boundaries mean 'not included'.

redesign.idea: Open-set tester: learner clicks points of a region; around each point the largest ball fitting inside is drawn, and boundary points visibly fail when the boundary is included.
redesign.interaction: Toggle region boundary between included and excluded; click points near the edge and watch whether a ball of positive radius fits.

figures.label: Fig. C.2 (g)
figures.caption_paraphrase: An open cover of a subset of the plane.
figures.visual_description: Inside a square frame, a cluster of about eight small overlapping dashed circles covers an irregular region.
figures.what_it_teaches: An open cover is a family of open sets whose union contains the set.

redesign.idea: Cover-building game: learner places discs to cover a shape, then tries to discard discs while keeping coverage; for an open interval near its missing endpoint a finite subcover cannot be found, previewing compactness.
redesign.interaction: Place and remove discs; a coverage meter and a 'finite subcover found?' indicator update.

figures.label: Fig. C.2 (h)
figures.caption_paraphrase: A non-Hausdorff space, pictured as branching.
figures.visual_description: Two thin grey rectangular sheets crossing each other at right angles, one roughly horizontal and one vertical, intersecting along a common line: a branching or forking surface.
figures.what_it_teaches: Spaces that branch fail the separation property the book assumes; such spaces are excluded.

redesign.idea: Line-with-two-origins demo: a real line whose origin is doubled; learner shrinks neighbourhoods of the two origins and sees they always overlap.
redesign.interaction: Slider shrinks neighbourhood radius; overlap region stays non-empty for the doubled origin but separates for ordinary distinct points.

figures.label: Fig. C.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: A function viewed as a map from one space to another.
figures.visual_description: Two irregular closed blobs labelled M (left) and N (right). A dot x in M is joined by a curved arrow labelled f to a dot f(x) in N.
figures.what_it_teaches: The abstract map picture used for every later construction.

redesign.idea: Reusable 'map card' component: drag a point in M and see its image move in N; used as the base widget for all later composite-map diagrams.
redesign.interaction: Drag x; f(x) follows; learner can swap f among a few preset maps.

figures.label: Fig. C.4 (a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: A many-to-one mapping.
figures.visual_description: Blob M (left) contains a small dotted shaded patch holding several points; a bundle of thin arrows from those points converges onto a single point in blob N (right).
figures.what_it_teaches: Several inputs can share one output, so the inverse image of a point need not be a point.

redesign.idea: Arrow-diagram classifier: learner draws arrows from dots in M to dots in N; badges for one-to-one, onto, bijective light up live.
redesign.interaction: Click-drag arrows between two finite dot sets; the classification and existence of an inverse update.

figures.label: Fig. C.4 (b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: An into mapping that is one-to-one but does not fill the target.
figures.visual_description: Blob M fully hatched; about eight arrows from distinct points land at distinct points clustered in a small lightly shaded part of blob N, leaving most of N unreached.
figures.what_it_teaches: A map defined on all of M can be one-to-one yet miss much of N (not onto).

redesign.idea: Same classifier widget with the target region shaded by coverage.
redesign.interaction: As above.

figures.label: Fig. C.4 (c)
figures.caption_paraphrase: A bijection: one-to-one and onto.
figures.visual_description: Both blobs fully hatched; parallel arrows pair each marked point of M with a distinct point of N spread across all of N.
figures.what_it_teaches: Bijections pair up points perfectly, so an inverse map exists.

redesign.idea: Same classifier widget; reversing all arrows produces the inverse map only when the bijection badge is lit.
redesign.interaction: Button 'reverse arrows'; widget explains why the reversed diagram fails to be a map in cases (a) and (b).

figures.label: Fig. C.5 (a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Graph of a one-to-one but not onto real function (caption misnumbers the example as C.5; it belongs to Example C.1).
figures.visual_description: x-y axes with a monotonically increasing curve that hugs a horizontal level just above the x-axis on the left and rises steeply on the right, like an exponential; it never reaches negative y.
figures.what_it_teaches: Strictly increasing means one-to-one; a range bounded below means not onto R.

redesign.idea: Horizontal-line-test explorer for real functions: learner sweeps a horizontal line and sees the number of intersections, plus shading of the unreached part of the y-axis.
redesign.interaction: Drag horizontal line; pick among exponential, cubic with wiggle, x^3, x^2 or type a formula; badges update.

figures.label: Fig. C.5 (b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Graph of an onto but not one-to-one function.
figures.visual_description: Axes with a cubic-like curve rising from the bottom left, making a small hump above the axis and a dip below near the origin, then rising steeply to the top right.
figures.what_it_teaches: Covers every y value but some values are hit three times.

redesign.idea: Covered by the horizontal-line-test explorer.
redesign.interaction: As above.

figures.label: Fig. C.5 (c)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Graph of a bijection.
figures.visual_description: Axes with an increasing curve that is flat at the origin (horizontal tangent) and steep far from it, like y = x^3, extending from the bottom left to the top right.
figures.what_it_teaches: Monotone and unbounded in both directions: one-to-one and onto. The same shape later reappears as the non-diffeomorphism x^3 of Example C.9.

redesign.idea: Add a toggle to the explorer that overlays the inverse function's graph and its derivative, showing the inverse's infinite slope at 0.
redesign.interaction: Toggle 'show inverse' and 'show derivative of inverse'.

figures.label: Fig. C.5 (d)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Graph of a function that is neither one-to-one nor onto.
figures.visual_description: Axes with an upward-opening parabola with its vertex at the origin.
figures.what_it_teaches: Even function hits each positive value twice and never reaches negative values.

redesign.idea: Covered by the horizontal-line-test explorer.
redesign.interaction: As above.

figures.label: Fig. C.6
figures.caption_paraphrase: Continuous deformation of a coffee mug with a handle into a doughnut; a handleless mug could not be deformed this way without making a hole.
figures.visual_description: Three hand-drawn objects separated by 'approximately equal' (homeomorphic) symbols: a mug with a handle, an intermediate squashed blob with a loop where the handle was, and a ring-shaped doughnut.
figures.what_it_teaches: Homeomorphism preserves the number of holes; stretching and squashing are allowed, tearing and gluing are not.

redesign.idea: 3D morph: a clay mug continuously morphs into a torus under a slider; a second object (handleless mug or sphere) tries to morph and a 'tear needed' warning appears at the step where a hole would have to be punched.
redesign.interaction: Scrub a morph slider; switch the start object; the hole count (genus) is displayed and stays fixed during legal deformations.

figures.label: Fig. C.7
figures.caption_paraphrase: Circle, sphere and torus each look locally like R or R^2 under magnification; the torus is a product of two circles.
figures.visual_description: (a) A circle labelled S^1 with a magnifying glass held against one point; an arrow leads to the lens showing a straight line labelled R. (b) A globe-like sphere S^2 with latitude and longitude lines and a magnifier showing a flat patch labelled R^2. (c) A shaded torus labelled T^2 = S^1 x S^1 with two bold circles (one around the tube, one around the hole) and a magnifier showing R^2.
figures.what_it_teaches: The defining property of a manifold is local flatness under sufficient magnification, not global flatness; product construction of the torus.

redesign.idea: Infinite-zoom manifold microscope: learner picks a space (circle, sphere, torus, double cone, plane with a spike) and zooms continuously on any point; for manifolds the view flattens, for non-manifolds the apex or junction never flattens.
redesign.interaction: Click a point, scroll to zoom; a flatness meter reports curvature of the visible patch; switch between manifold and non-manifold objects.

figures.label: Fig. C.8
figures.caption_paraphrase: A chart map sends an open patch of the manifold to a region of R^m.
figures.visual_description: Left: an irregular blob M containing a smaller curvilinear patch U drawn with a distorted grid. A curved arrow labelled phi leads to a boxed panel labelled R^m containing a region phi(U) with a straightened rectangular grid.
figures.what_it_teaches: Coordinates are a map from part of the manifold to number space; the grid on U is the pullback of the Cartesian grid.

redesign.idea: Chart mapper: on a sphere, the learner drags a patch U; the right panel shows its image under a chosen chart (angles, stereographic), with gridlines linked by hover.
redesign.interaction: Drag or resize U on the 3D sphere; hover a grid point to highlight its coordinate image; switch chart types and watch the image deform; patches that include a pole show the chart failing.

figures.label: Fig. C.9 (a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: The angle chart phi_1 sends points of patch U_1 on the unit circle to theta in R.
figures.visual_description: A bold circle inside a thin concentric outline labelled U_1, with the point P marked on its right-hand side where the outline has a small break. A curved arrow labelled phi_1 runs from near P to a vertical bar whose bottom end is theta = 0 and top end is theta = 2 pi.
figures.what_it_teaches: Angular coordinate as a chart on S^1.

redesign.idea: Two-chart circle atlas: a point moves around the circle while two number lines show its theta coordinate in chart 1 (0 to 2 pi) and chart 2 (-pi to pi); each chart's excluded point is drawn as a hollow circle, and the overlap transition map is plotted.
redesign.interaction: Drag the point around the circle; watch chart 1 jump at P and chart 2 jump at Q; a third panel plots theta_2 versus theta_1 on the overlap (two line segments with a shift of 2 pi).

figures.label: Fig. C.9 (b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: The problem point: the same position on the circle would be assigned both 0 and 2 pi, so it must be removed from U_1.
figures.visual_description: The bold circle with the thin surrounding outline U_1 now drawn as a loop that stops short at one point; two curved arrows from that same point go to both the theta = 0 end and the theta = 2 pi end of the vertical bar.
figures.what_it_teaches: A single chart on the circle cannot be one-to-one and onto an open interval; one point must be dropped.

redesign.idea: Part of the two-chart atlas demo: when the learner forces a single chart to include P, both endpoints of the interval light up and a 'not a function' warning appears.
redesign.interaction: Toggle 'include P in U_1'.

figures.label: Fig. C.9 (c)
figures.caption_paraphrase: A second chart phi_2 with values in (-pi, pi) omits a different point Q.
figures.visual_description: The bold circle with surrounding outline U_2; a point Q marked on the left side; a curved arrow phi_2 from a point near the top to a vertical bar labelled theta = -pi at the bottom and theta = pi at the top.
figures.what_it_teaches: Two charts with different missing points together cover the circle.

redesign.idea: Part of the two-chart atlas demo.
redesign.interaction: As in Fig. C.9(a).

figures.label: Fig. C.10
figures.caption_paraphrase: A coordinate transformation built from two overlapping charts.
figures.visual_description: Left: blob M containing two overlapping ovals U (upper) and V (lower); a point P sits in the hatched overlap. Right: a box R^m containing two regions phi(U) (upper) and psi(V) (lower), each with a hatched overlap image containing the labelled points x^mu and y^mu. Arrows: phi from U to phi(U); psi from V to psi(V); phi^{-1}(x) from x^mu back to P; psi(P) from P to y^mu.
figures.what_it_teaches: The transition map is phi^{-1} followed by psi, defined only on the overlap.

redesign.idea: Transition-map tracer: on a sphere covered by two stereographic charts, the learner picks a point in chart 1's plane; an animated path goes up to the sphere and down into chart 2's plane, while the explicit formula y = x/|x|^2 is evaluated live.
redesign.interaction: Drag the point in chart 1; the traced path and the chart-2 coordinates update; moving outside the overlap greys out the transition.

figures.label: Fig. C.11
figures.caption_paraphrase: A function on the manifold is handled through its composite with the inverse chart.
figures.visual_description: Blob M with patch U and point P inside. An arrow f runs from P to a point on a vertical real line R at the top right. An arrow phi runs down from P to a point x in a coordinate plane R^m at the bottom left. A curved arrow labelled f o phi^{-1}(x) runs from x to the same point on R, closing a commuting triangle.
figures.what_it_teaches: The familiar f(x^1,...,x^m) is a coordinate representation; the manifold function is chart independent.

redesign.idea: Temperature on a globe: a scalar field is painted on a sphere; two chart panels (latitude-longitude and stereographic) show different-looking formulas and contour plots of the same field, with a probe point linked across all three views.
redesign.interaction: Move the probe on any view; the value readout is identical in all three while the coordinate formulas differ.

figures.label: Fig. C.12
figures.caption_paraphrase: A map between manifolds and its coordinate representation.
figures.visual_description: Two blobs M (left) and N (right), each with a patch (U containing P; V containing f(P)). An arrow f joins P to f(P). Arrows phi and psi go down to two gridded patches in coordinate planes R^m (left, point x) and R^m (right, point y). A curved arrow labelled psi o f o phi^{-1} joins x to y.
figures.what_it_teaches: Maps between manifolds are studied through the chart sandwich psi o f o phi^{-1}; differentiability is defined this way.

redesign.idea: Commuting-square widget: learner chooses f (a rotation of the sphere, a squash) and charts on both sides; the lower arrow's formula and Jacobian are computed, and changing either chart changes the formula but not the upper map.
redesign.interaction: Select map and charts; drag a point; display psi o f o phi^{-1} numerically and its Jacobian determinant.

figures.label: Fig. C.13
figures.caption_paraphrase: A curve on the manifold and its coordinate image.
figures.visual_description: Left: a vertical interval from a (bottom) to b (top) with a point lambda. An arrow c goes from lambda to a point c(lambda) on a short curve drawn inside patch U of blob M. An arrow phi descends to a curve in a coordinate plane R^m; a long curved arrow phi o c goes directly from lambda to the corresponding point in R^m.
figures.what_it_teaches: Curves are maps from an interval, and their coordinate description is a composite.

redesign.idea: Curve scrubber: a slider for lambda moves a bead along a curve on a torus; the chart panel shows the same bead moving along x^mu(lambda), and the reparametrization control shows the same image traced at different speeds.
redesign.interaction: Drag lambda slider; choose reparametrization lambda -> lambda^2 or 2 lambda; observe unchanged image but changed velocity.

figures.label: Fig. C.14
figures.caption_paraphrase: A tangent vector expressed through maps: curve, function, and chart.
figures.visual_description: An interval from a to b with 0 marked on the left. Arrow c sends 0 to c(0) on a curve in patch U of blob M; a short arrow X is tangent at c(0), and another point c(t) lies along the curve. Arrow f goes from the curve to a vertical real line R on the right. Arrow phi goes down to a point in R^m; arrow phi o c goes from the interval to that point; arrow f o phi^{-1} goes from R^m up to R.
figures.what_it_teaches: The derivative of f o c factors through coordinate space, which is where the chain rule and components come from.

redesign.idea: Directional-derivative lab: a scalar field on a curved surface and a curve through P; the learner changes the function or the curve and watches d(f o c)/dlambda computed both directly and as (dx^mu/dlambda)(partial f/partial x^mu) with matching bars.
redesign.interaction: Drag the curve's direction at P and switch functions; two numeric readouts (direct and chain-rule) stay equal; curves with the same velocity at P give identical readouts.

figures.label: Fig. C.15
figures.caption_paraphrase: (a) Many vectors in the tangent space at a point; (b) the embedded tangent-plane picture used earlier in the book.
figures.visual_description: (a) A pair of perpendicular axes, off to one side, beside a point P from which about eight short arrows radiate in different directions, with no surface drawn. (b) A hand-drawn gridded dome (like part of a globe) with a flat rectangular card touching it at P; the same starburst of arrows lies in the card.
figures.what_it_teaches: Tangent vectors at P form a vector space; the familiar tangent plane is an embedding-dependent visualization of it.

redesign.idea: Intrinsic versus embedded tangent space: split view where the right shows the tangent plane on an embedded sphere and the left shows only the abstract 2D vector space with basis partial_theta, partial_phi; changing the embedding (sphere to ellipsoid) moves the plane but leaves the abstract space and components unchanged.
redesign.interaction: Deform the embedding with a slider; pick a curve through P; the vector's components in the abstract panel stay put while the 3D arrow tilts.

figures.label: Fig. C.16
figures.caption_paraphrase: (a) Tangent lines to a wavy one-dimensional manifold at several points; (b) the same tangents redrawn as vertical lines, the fibres of a bundle.
figures.visual_description: (a) A bold sinusoidal curve with points p (a crest), q (a trough) and r (a later crest); straight tangent lines at each point extend far enough to cross one another. (b) The same wavy curve with vertical lines through p, q and r.
figures.what_it_teaches: Drawing tangent spaces in place causes overlaps; rotating them to stand vertically separates them and suggests the bundle construction.

redesign.idea: Animated 'comb the tangents': tangent lines on a curve rotate to vertical and the curve straightens into a base line, producing the fibres of TM; the learner can pick a tangent vector at each point and see it become a bead height.
redesign.interaction: Play/scrub the rotation animation; click points to set tangent-vector lengths, which become beads on fibres.

figures.label: Fig. C.17
figures.caption_paraphrase: A bundle B made of fibres V above a base M, with the projection pi collapsing each fibre to a point.
figures.visual_description: A dense row of about 25 parallel vertical line segments labelled B; small arrows point to a few of them with the label V. A downward arrow labelled pi points to a horizontal line labelled M below.
figures.what_it_teaches: Total space, fibre, base and projection.

redesign.idea: Bundle anatomy explorer: hover any point of the total space to highlight its fibre and its projected base point; toggle the fibre type (R, circle, finite set).
redesign.interaction: Hover and click; switch fibre type to see the total space change (strip, torus, disjoint copies).

figures.label: Fig. C.18
figures.caption_paraphrase: A product bundle M x V and its projection.
figures.visual_description: A tall rectangle ruled into a grid, labelled M x V, with a dot marking the point at horizontal position a and vertical position b. Below, a row of thick downward arrows points to a hatched horizontal bar labelled M.
figures.what_it_teaches: Points of a trivial bundle are pairs (a, b); projection keeps a.

redesign.idea: Fold into the bundle anatomy explorer with a 'product coordinates' overlay.
redesign.interaction: Drag the point and read (a, b) and pi(a, b) = a.

figures.label: Fig. C.19
figures.caption_paraphrase: The tangent bundle of the circle as a cylinder floating above the circle.
figures.visual_description: A cylinder drawn with many vertical line segments (solid at the front, dashed at the back) labelled TS^1, above a separate flat ellipse labelled S^1.
figures.what_it_teaches: TS^1 is globally the product of the circle with a line: a cylinder.

redesign.idea: 3D cylinder bundle: a point circles the base while a vector (arrow tangent to the circle) at that point is shown both as an arrow on the circle and as a bead on the cylinder's fibre above it; drawing a vector field paints a closed curve on the cylinder.
redesign.interaction: Orbit camera; drag beads on fibres to set the vector field; the tangent arrows on the base update.

figures.label: Fig. C.20 (a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: The globally trivial bundle over the circle.
figures.visual_description: Photograph of a physical model: a thin white ring with about 30 straight black rods passing through it, all standing vertically and parallel, forming a cylindrical fence.
figures.what_it_teaches: Fibres stay aligned all the way round: a cylinder.

redesign.idea: Twist slider over the circle: rods start vertical (cylinder) and a slider sets the total rotation of the fibres around the loop; allowed end values are 0 or a half turn (mod a full turn) to close up, giving cylinder or Moebius.
redesign.interaction: Drag the twist slider; snap to closed configurations; orbit the 3D view; toggle a surface skin to reveal cylinder or Moebius strip.

figures.label: Fig. C.20 (b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: The twisted bundle, whose fibres form a Moebius strip.
figures.visual_description: Photograph of the same ring with black rods, but the rods tilt progressively as one goes around the ring, fanning outward and turning over through half a revolution so that the rods trace out a Moebius band.
figures.what_it_teaches: Locally each rod has neighbours nearly parallel to it (local product), but globally the fibres come back flipped.

redesign.idea: Same twist-slider model as panel (a).
redesign.interaction: As above.

figures.label: Fig. C.21
figures.caption_paraphrase: A cross section: the base lifted into the bundle as a curve meeting every fibre once, like the graph of a function.
figures.visual_description: A cylinder labelled B drawn with dashed horizontal ellipses; a bold wavy closed curve winds once around its middle and a lighter dotted wavy curve runs near the top rim. Below, an ellipse labelled M carries several upward arrows labelled s pointing toward the cylinder.
figures.what_it_teaches: Sections pick one fibre point over each base point; on a product bundle they are graphs of functions.

redesign.idea: Section painter with zero-section test: learner draws a section on the cylinder or the Moebius band by dragging control points; the zero section is drawn in red and crossings are counted; on the Moebius band the counter never reaches zero.
redesign.interaction: Drag heights of control points around the loop; switch between cylinder and Moebius; a crossing counter and an 'avoids zero?' badge update.

worked_examples.label: Example C.1
worked_examples.problem: Classify four real functions drawn as graphs as one-to-one, onto, both, or neither.
worked_examples.method: Inspect each graph: monotonicity for injectivity, whether all y values are reached for surjectivity.
worked_examples.key_insight: Graph shape alone decides the classification; a bijection needs both strict monotonicity (for continuous functions) and unbounded range.
worked_examples.result: (a) exponential-like: 1-1 not onto; (b) wiggly cubic: onto not 1-1; (c) x^3-like: bijection; (d) parabola: neither.

worked_examples.label: Example C.2
worked_examples.problem: Decide for several pairs of spaces whether they are homeomorphic.
worked_examples.method: Apply the continuous-deformation picture and topological invariants (dimension, number of holes, compactness).
worked_examples.key_insight: Homeomorphism ignores shape details but respects holes, dimension and compactness.
worked_examples.result: Homeomorphic: open disc and open square; graph of a differentiable function and its domain; parameter interval and a differentiably parametrized curve; mug and doughnut. Not homeomorphic: R^m and R^n with m different from n; the real line and the circle (circle compact, line not).

worked_examples.label: Example C.3
worked_examples.problem: List spaces that are and are not manifolds.
worked_examples.method: Check local resemblance to R^n at every point.
worked_examples.key_insight: A single bad point (junction, cone apex) is enough to disqualify a space.
worked_examples.result: Manifolds: R^m, S^1, S^2, T^2. Not manifolds: a plane with a line sticking out; a double cone.

worked_examples.label: Example C.4
worked_examples.problem: Try to cover the unit circle with a single angle coordinate running from 0 to 2 pi.
worked_examples.method: Map points to theta; notice the starting point receives both 0 and 2 pi; restore one-to-oneness by deleting that point from the chart domain.
worked_examples.key_insight: Global topology (the circle closes up) prevents a single homeomorphism onto an open interval.
worked_examples.result: U_1 = circle minus P; phi_1 is a valid chart there.

worked_examples.label: Example C.5
worked_examples.problem: Complete the covering of the unit circle.
worked_examples.method: Define a second angle chart with values in (-pi, pi), which omits a different point Q, and check that the two domains together contain every point.
worked_examples.key_insight: Two charts with different excluded points suffice; overlaps are where transition maps live.

worked_examples.label: Example C.6
worked_examples.problem: How many charts are needed for Euclidean space and for the two one-dimensional manifolds?
worked_examples.method: Use the identity chart for R^m and R; recall the circle argument.
worked_examples.key_insight: The minimum number of charts reflects global topology, not local structure.
worked_examples.result: R^m and the line: one chart; the circle: at least two.

worked_examples.label: Example C.7
worked_examples.problem: Give the coordinate representation of a map f between two m-dimensional manifolds.
worked_examples.method: Choose charts (U, phi) around P and (V, psi) around f(P) and compose psi o f o phi^{-1}.
worked_examples.key_insight: Any map between manifolds becomes an ordinary tuple-valued function once charts are fixed on both sides.

worked_examples.problem: Show why differentiability of f judged in one chart need not persist in another chart.
